extracted.intended_audience: postsecondary mathematics instructors, mathematics educators, and graduate students interested in equitable teaching
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical/analytic standards for recognizing and disrupting social hierarchies and inequities in undergraduate mathematics classrooms, including observational methods (EQUIP) and instructional practices. Emphasizes measuring participation, attending to Discourses/status, and pairing active-learning methods with equity work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disrupt hierarchies in the classroom
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless you actively disrupt the hierarchies created by larger systems of oppression, you may unintentionally reproduce them in your classroom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors must intentionally disrupt classroom hierarchies (status, Discourses) via pedagogical moves and co-created norms; otherwise active participation will concentrate among a small subset of students. Work is ongoing and requires unlearning oppressive Discourses over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pair active learning with equity work
rubrics_metrics.description: Trying to create an active learning environment without simultaneously disrupting these hierarchies likely means only a small subset of your class will get to actively engage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When implementing active-engagement techniques, explicitly attend to who participates and who benefits; use techniques (e.g., status-mitigating instructional moves) to ensure active learning does not exacerbate inequities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use equity analytics (EQUIP) to track participation
rubrics_metrics.description: EQUIP is an observation tool and methodology for tracking patterns of student participation to reveal classroom hierarchies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize participation empirically: collect observational data, disaggregate by student groups, and use results to identify and target inequitable patterns. EQUIP supports data-driven professional development to change participation patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalize equity via equality as a waypoint (reparations view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw upon the concept of equality as a waypoint towards equity: if minoritized students receive fewer opportunities to participate relative to peers, that signifies inequity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use equal share of participation opportunities (or reparative increases) as a measurable indicator to guide interventions even if a full definition of equity is contested. Aim to repair historical and present harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track multiple participation modalities, not just verbal
rubrics_metrics.description: While much work focuses on verbal talk, EQUIP and similar approaches capture written, gesture, ASL, manipulatives, and other modalities of public mathematical expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include any public expression of mathematical ideas when coding participation; customize methodology to capture modality diversity so that non-verbal contributions are recognized and counted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a strengths-based mindset: assume all students are brilliant
rubrics_metrics.description: I take as an axiom that all students are brilliant and capable of success; rather than noticing deficits, develop a mindset of seeing what your students can do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build instruction on student strengths, avoid deficit framings that reproduce low expectations, and design tasks and supports that expand access rather than labeling students as incapable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a safe and inviting environment for marginalized students
rubrics_metrics.description: Your job is to create a safe and inviting environment that supports all your students—especially those at the margins—to be meaningfully involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume reasons for nonparticipation (could be access, anxiety, trauma); provide access to materials, reduce barriers, attend to belonging cues (classroom decor, norms), and proactively support mental and material needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to Discourses and status in classroom interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Discourses (collections of signs, narratives, and norms) constrain subject positions; status determines whose ideas carry weight in discussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify dominant Discourses (e.g., who is positioned as 'good at math'), monitor status imbalances (who speaks, who gets hard questions), and use instructional moves to treat status (e.g., equitable call patterns, highlight contributions from marginalized students) to disrupt oppressive Discourses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigate stereotype threat and limit reliance on high-stakes timed exams
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotype threat occurs when negatively stereotyped students face high-stress assessments; high-stakes timed exams can reinforce inequities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that stereotype threat has measurable effects; adopt alternative assessment practices, lower situational stress, and design assessments that reduce activation of negative stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid microaggressions and low expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Microaggressions are toxic interpersonal interactions grounded in social identities; low expectations by instructors materially reduce student opportunities and performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of subtle cues (surprised comments, who is praised or reprimanded), actively counteract biased expectations, and ensure equitable access to mentoring, opportunities, and affirming interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect and disaggregate student data to inform professional development
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional development methods grounded in disaggregated student data can reliably produce changes to patterns of inequity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use disaggregated participation data (by race, gender, disability, etc.) to pinpoint inequities, then design PD that addresses specific patterns; iteratively measure impact to refine interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize interventions for local hierarchies and intersectionality
rubrics_metrics.description: The exact hierarchies and systems of oppression vary by context; Discourses intersect with multiple identities (race, gender, disability, class, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use local knowledge to identify salient hierarchies (e.g., pure vs applied math, regional cultural factors), attend to intersectional experiences, and tailor disruption strategies accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure equitable distribution of high-quality participation opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation opportunities (who is called on, who receives higher-level questions) are strongly related to learning; biases lead privileged students to get more and better opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor not just quantity of talk but quality of opportunities (complexity of questions, chances for follow-up). Intentionally allocate high-level tasks and questioning to historically marginalized students to equalize learning access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code student contributions using clear segmentation rules (EQUIP coding rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic unit of analysis is a student contribution: for verbal contributions, analyze all talk from a single student that is not interrupted by another student; follow-up prompts by the instructor to the same student can be part of the same contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment observations by contributions so every coded behavior attaches to a specific contribution. Start a new contribution when a new student speaks. This allows aggregation/disaggregation by student and group for analytic comparisons.
